title: Blurred Vision in a Taxi Driver with Diabetes / Grade the Eye, Check He Can Drive

blocks.text: Blurred Vision in a Taxi Driver with Diabetes / Grade the Eye, Check He Can Drive

AMaC MRCP PACES · R2-56 · Consultation · PACES Station 5, consultation encounter · Skills A, B, C, D, E, F, G (all seven) · 20 min: 15 min with the patient, then 5 min of examiner questions; warning at 13 min · Guidelines: NICE NG28 Type 2 diabetes in adults: management (published 2 December 2015; last updated 18 February 2026); gov.uk, Eye conditions and driving (page accessed October 2026); gov.uk, NHS Diabetic Eye Screening Programme: features-based grading outcomes guidance (updated 4 December 2025) · Related AMaC: Consultation: hypoglycaemia and driving

Dear Doctor, a 56-year-old taxi driver. Type 2 diabetes for 12 years on metformin and gliclazide. Blurred vision in the right eye for three weeks. HbA1c 84 mmol/mol, BP 156/94. Missed his last eye screening. Please assess and advise.
Please take a history, perform a relevant examination, including looking at the fundi, and explain your assessment and plan to the patient.

sections.heading: 4. The Hook and the Examiner Trap

blocks.text: The Hook. Blurred vision in poorly controlled diabetes with a missed screening visit is diabetic eye disease until the eye specialists show otherwise; describe what you see, refer urgently, and ask whether he can still meet the driving standard.

The Examiner Trap. He wants new glasses and says he is fine to drive. Candidates agree. Pass: examine the fundi, name the retinopathy and maculopathy, refer urgently, advise on driving. Fail: say he can keep driving the taxi.

rows: Eye disease or a glucose swing? Get the story.

Look at the eye and the whole picture.
"May I check your vision, look into your eyes and take your blood pressure?"
Acuity, fields, pupils, fundi, BP, feet, urine.
"I can see bleeds and fatty deposits near the centre of the retina. You need an urgent eye clinic review."

Share the plan; find his worry.
Explain risks, options, safety net; check understanding.

No vision, glucose or driving history

Adds cotton wool spots, venous beading, fields, pupils and BP, and states negatives: no new vessels, no vitreous bleed

Explains that, because he has symptoms, he goes straight to the hospital eye service rather than waiting for screening, and that sudden loss of vision, new floaters or a curtain need same-day assessment; also an individual HbA1c target, BP treatment and review of drugs

Advises that vision must meet the standard and not to drive unless legal visual standards are met

blocks.text: High-performance is an AMaC teaching label, not an official grade. It shows what lifts a pass from adequate to convincing. Critical fail is an AMaC practice flag for an action that could harm the patient today; it is not an official automatic PACES fail.
Who you are. A 56-year-old taxi driver. Practical, defensive about work, anxious. Married, two children.
Opening line. "My right eye is blurry. I just need new glasses. I'm fine to drive."
Volunteered. Blurred vision in the right eye for three weeks.

Only if asked. A dark shadow floating at times. No flashes or pain. Last eye screening three years ago. Tablets irregularly. Smoker. No hypoglycaemia. No kidney problems known. No blood pressure tablets or statin. You drink about two pints at weekends. Your father had diabetes. No recent travel. Married with two children; you are the main earner. You drive about nine hours a day and struggled to read a sign this week. No allergies.
Hidden concern. You fear losing your taxi licence and your sight. Reveal only if asked what worries you most.
Your questions. "Can I keep driving?" "Will I go blind?" "Do I need laser?" "Is it my sugar?"
How you react. Good handling: you agree to stop driving until assessed. Poor handling: if told you cannot work you say you will drive anyway.

Findings (released as each step is done). Visual acuity right eye 6/18, left 6/9 (scenario values). Pupils equal and reactive. Right fundus: dot and blot haemorrhages, hard exudates close to the macula, two cotton wool spots, venous beading in two quadrants; no new vessels. Left fundus: scattered dot haemorrhages. BP 156/94. HbA1c 84 mmol/mol. Feet: reduced sensation. Urine: protein 1+.

Question ladder. Q1 Diagnosis and grade (R4, R5): diabetic retinopathy with maculopathy in the right eye, with features of pre-proliferative change (cotton wool spots, venous beading); the exact grade needs retinal imaging and assessment by the eye service. Q2 Management (R6): urgent referral straight to hospital eye services (he is symptomatic with reduced acuity, so not the routine screening pathway); HbA1c target agreed individually (NICE NG28: 53 mmol/mol is the usual aim on a drug that can cause hypoglycaemia, such as gliclazide, relaxed case by case); BP treatment. Q3 Risk (R5): proliferative change, vitreous bleed. Q4 Driving (R7): must read a number plate from 20 metres; tell DVLA if the condition affects both eyes, if retinopathy is treated with laser, or if a doctor, optician or eye specialist says he should not drive or may not meet the standard (gov.uk). Taxi licences are issued by the local authority, which may set its own medical standard. Q5 Other (R6): kidney, feet, smoking.
Curveball 1. "He sees sudden flashes and a curtain." (R6) Safe: retinal detachment; same-day eye emergency.
Curveball 2. "He cannot read the number plate." (R7) Safe: must not drive; tell DVLA as advised.
Curveball 3. "The screening grade is R3." (R5) Safe: proliferative; urgent referral.
Curveball 4. "I'll keep driving." (R7) Safe: explain the law and risk; document; revisit.

Fail performance
CANDIDATE: I'll shine a light in your eye. [R1 Fail] (No driving history. [R2 Fail] [R3 Fail])
(Reports new vessels that are not there. [R4 Fail])
CANDIDATE: You need glasses. [R5 Fail] See the optician. [R6 Fail]
CANDIDATE: You're fine to drive. [R7 Fail]

Examiner note: No history, signs invented and no referral. Telling him he is fine to drive with reduced vision is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): a collision can injure him and others.
Pass performance
CANDIDATE: Hello. May I check your vision and look in your eyes? I'll warn you before the light. [R1 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Tell me about the vision: when it started, any pain, floaters or flashes. How have your sugars been, and when was your last eye screening? Do you drive for work? [R2 Pass]
PATIENT: I drive a taxi. I'm afraid of losing my licence and my sight.
CANDIDATE: That's a real worry. What concerns you most? [R3 Pass]
(Checks acuity, pupils, fundi and BP; finds reduced right acuity, haemorrhages and exudates, no new vessels. [R4 Pass])
CANDIDATE: This is diabetic retinopathy with maculopathy. [R5 Pass]

CANDIDATE: I'll refer you urgently to the hospital eye service rather than wait for routine screening, and we'll agree targets for sugar and blood pressure. If your sight suddenly worsens, or you see new floaters, flashes or a curtain, come in the same day. [R6 Pass]
CANDIDATE: Your vision must meet the driving standard. Until checked, you should not drive. Do you understand? [R7 Pass]
Examiner note: Safe and clear. Did not name the number plate rule or who tells DVLA.
High-performance performance
CANDIDATE: May I offer a chaperone? I'll dim the lights and tell you each step. [R1 High]
CANDIDATE: Any hypoglycaemia, smoking or kidney problems? How is your work affected? [R2 High]
PATIENT: I'm afraid of losing my licence and going blind.
CANDIDATE: Thank you for telling me. Early treatment protects your sight, and we'll tell you where you stand with driving. [R3 High]
(Also finds cotton wool spots and venous beading; no new vessels or vitreous bleed. [R4 High])
CANDIDATE: Pre-proliferative retinopathy with maculopathy in the right eye; cataract and proliferative disease are alternatives. [R5 High]
CANDIDATE: Urgent hospital eye review; an individual HbA1c target agreed with you per NICE; treating your blood pressure; and checking your kidneys and feet. [R6 High]

CANDIDATE: You must be able to read a number plate from 20 metres; if not, don't drive. Tell DVLA if the condition affects both eyes, if you need laser, or if you're told you may not meet the standard, and check with your licensing authority; the eye specialist will assess. Thank you for letting me examine you. [R7 High] [R1 High]
Examiner note: Graded the eye, referred and gave exact driving advice.
R7: Telling a taxi driver with reduced vision he can drive is a Critical fail (AMaC practice flag, not an official automatic PACES fail): a collision can injure him and others.
R2: Not asking about driving or screening misses the risk.
R4: Reporting new vessels not present shows signs were assumed.
R5: Calling it glasses ignores haemorrhages and exudates.
R6: No referral leaves sight-threatening disease untreated.
"Do you drive for work?"
"I'd refer you urgently to the eye clinic."
"What worries you most?"

NICE NG28 (published 2 December 2015; last updated 18 February 2026): HbA1c targets are agreed individually, usually 53 mmol/mol (7.0%) for adults on a drug associated with hypoglycaemia; the blood pressure section sits in the NICE hypertension guideline.
gov.uk, Eye conditions and driving (page accessed October 2026). https://www.gov.uk/eye-conditions-and-driving Supports: number plate standard; duty to tell DVLA.

Screening grades (features-based grading, updated 4 December 2025): R1 background; R2L lower-risk pre-proliferative (digital surveillance); R2H higher-risk pre-proliferative, which includes venous beading in two or more quadrants (routine hospital eye services); R3A active proliferative (urgent hospital eye services); M1 referable maculopathy. These grades guide screening of people without new symptoms. A symptomatic patient with reduced acuity, like this patient, needs prompt assessment by the eye service and should not wait for the screening pathway. Sudden loss of vision, a new shower of floaters, flashes or a curtain need same-day eye emergency assessment.
THINK: Diabetic eye disease; can he drive?
SAY: "I can see bleeds near the centre; you need an urgent eye clinic."
DO: Acuity; fundi; BP; refer; targets; driving advice.
NUMBERS: Acuity 6/18, HbA1c 84 mmol/mol, BP 156/94 (scenario); number plate 20 m (gov.uk).
TRAP: Glasses and "fine to drive".
FINISH: Direct urgent eye referral; sudden loss, new floaters, flashes or a curtain: same-day eye emergency.
